speaker: John Schulman
title: John Schulman (OpenAI Cofounder) — Reasoning, RLHF, & plan for 2027 AGI
question: In LLM post-training, why isn't a single round of supervised fine-tuning on high-quality human-written data enough to build a strong chat assistant?
guest: I don't think you would be able to do just one iteration of fine-tuning where you have purely human-written data and you fine-tune on that. I think you would want to do several iterations. If you're not going to do RL, which we did, you'd want to do some kind of iterative supervised fine-tuning where you have humans edit the model-generated outputs. If you train on human-generated data, even if it's really high quality, it's just hard for a model to fit that data perfectly because it might not be something the model is capable of outputting. So you need to do something iterative that looks a little bit more like RL.

points.core: Models struggle to fit purely human-written data even at high quality.
points.note: Accept: models cannot cleanly imitate or memorize off-policy human-authored demonstrations regardless of writing quality. Do not credit: generic claims that more data is better or that humans make typos.

points.core: Human-authored demonstrations often fall outside what the model can naturally output.
points.note: Accept: distribution mismatch, capability gap, or off-policy targets that the base model cannot reliably generate itself. Do not credit: vague mentions of overfitting without tying it to output-capability mismatch.

points.core: Effective post-training requires multiple iterative rounds rather than one pass.
points.note: Accept: multi-round fine-tuning loops, repeated training iterations, or iterative refinement instead of single-shot SFT. Do not credit: generic advice to train for more epochs on the same static dataset.

points.core: Without RL, humans should iteratively edit outputs generated by the model.
points.note: Accept: having annotators revise, correct, or refine the model's own generations to create on-policy targets approximating RL. Do not credit: merely mentioning RLHF without explaining human editing of model-generated outputs.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Supervised fine-tuning teaches a model to imitate demonstrations, and imitation alone has several limits.

First, human-written data is expensive and scarce, so it can't cover the huge space of prompts, tasks, and edge cases an assistant faces; the model generalizes poorly outside that coverage.

Second, SFT trains on token-level likelihood under teacher forcing, so the model never learns from its own outputs. At inference, small errors compound into states the demonstrations never showed, and nothing teaches it to recover.

Third, imitation optimizes "what a human would write," not "what is the best response." It weights all tokens equally, can't express that one answer is better than another, and caps quality near the demonstrators' level. Preferences are also much easier for people to judge than to author, which is why preference-based methods (RLHF, DPO, reward models) add signal SFT can't.

Fourth, SFT can encourage hallucination: if a demonstration contains facts the model doesn't know, it learns to assert confidently anyway, since the target reflects the writer's knowledge, not the model's.

So strong assistants typically layer SFT with preference optimization or RL, synthetic data, and iterative rounds targeting observed failures.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone relies on behavior cloning via token-level maximum likelihood, which teaches a model to imitate style and format but leaves critical gaps. First, SFT provides only positive examples without negative feedback: its objective penalizes minor phrasing differences on par with factual errors or unsafe tokens, offering no direct pressure against subtle failure modes like sycophancy, over-refusal, or adversarial jailbreaks. Second, because SFT trains off-policy on human-written prefixes rather than the model's own generations, small mistakes compound during autoregressive decoding, and forcing the model to mimic answers containing facts outside its pretraining knowledge actively trains it to guess and hallucinate rather than abstain. Third, human demonstrations hit a quality and scalability ceiling, since verifying code, math, or relative response quality is far easier than authoring optimal responses from scratch. Iterative post-training with preference optimization and reinforcement learning overcomes these limits by evaluating complete on-policy generations, supplying contrastive and verifiable sequence-level rewards that calibrate uncertainty, balance helpfulness with safety, and unlock reasoning beyond human demonstrations.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: A single round of SFT on human-written data runs into several limits at once. First, imitation only teaches the model to copy demonstrations. It never learns which of its own outputs are better or worse, so it gets no signal against its specific failure modes like hallucination, sycophancy or unsafe completions. Second, there's a distribution mismatch. Humans write in their own style and from their own knowledge, so the model learns to imitate answers it can't actually produce, which can encourage confident fabrication. Training on the model's own sampled outputs, which RLHF, DPO and rejection sampling do, fixes this. Third, humans are often better at judging responses than writing them, especially for long or expert answers. Preference comparisons are cheaper and scale further than demonstrations, and they can push quality past what the annotators could write themselves. Finally, as the model improves, older data falls below its level. That's why recipes like Llama 2/3 and Tülu 3 run several rounds: SFT, then collecting preferences on the new model's outputs, then preference optimization or RL, repeated, often with verifiable rewards added for math and code.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A single round of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) teaches a model to imitate high-quality human responses, but imitation alone has fundamental limits. Because SFT optimizes token-level cross-entropy on positive examples only, it provides no negative feedback showing which mistakes, unsafe completions, or subtle failure modes to avoid. It also trains off-policy: the model learns from human-written trajectories rather than its own generations, creating a distribution shift at inference time where small errors can compound into hallucinations, repetition, or unhelpful behavior. Furthermore, forcing a model to mimic knowledgeable human answers can encourage it to hallucinate confidently when a prompt exceeds its pre-trained knowledge, rather than expressing uncertainty. Finally, SFT weights every token equally, whereas assistant quality depends heavily on holistic, sequence-level tradeoffs like helpfulness, honesty, tone, and safety. Preference optimization and reinforcement learning (such as RLHF, DPO, or verifiable-reward RL) address these gaps by evaluating and refining the model’s own outputs against explicit quality criteria.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Supervised fine-tuning teaches a model to imitate good answers, but even excellent demonstrations cover only a fraction of what users will ask. Each example shows one way to respond and gives little direct feedback about other plausible responses. During training, the model also learns to continue human-written text. In a live conversation, it has to continue from its own responses, including any mistakes it has already made.

Further post-training can address gaps that appear when the model is used. Human preference feedback can teach it which of several plausible answers is more helpful. Verifiable feedback, such as whether generated code passes tests, can reward correctness even when the solution differs from a demonstration. Evaluating the model and collecting new examples around its actual failures helps it improve on cases the original dataset missed.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Supervised fine-tuning teaches a model to imitate good answers. But even excellent human-written examples cover only a fraction of the conversations an assistant will face. For each prompt, the model learns to predict the words in one demonstration. That gives it little direct feedback on which of several plausible replies is most helpful, accurate, or appropriate. In a multi-turn chat, its own replies can also steer the conversation into situations the demonstrations never covered.

Preference training adds a different signal. Evaluators can compare two replies the model actually produced and favor the one that caught a false premise, asked a needed clarification, or explained the answer more clearly. Testing the updated model then reveals which mistakes persist and where more demonstrations or feedback would help. A single supervised round can produce a capable assistant, but its training signal alone gives limited guidance on the choices that make one plausible reply better than another.
